item.title: In Scotland, a (Very Posh) Summer Camp for Grown-Ups
item.description:
There comes a time in every English summer when posh friends take off for the countryside, for long weekends in mansions they refer to as “cottages.” Luckily, there’s a place for the rest of us longing for storybook getaways, too.

It’s called Gleneagles.

About an hour outside of Edinburgh, it’s a luxury hotel, one built in the manner of the great Scottish castles and billing itself as “the Glorious Playground.” It’s the mix of lush adventures by day and elegant dinners by night that we began dreaming about from the moment our stay was booked. A lot of high-end hotels offer beautiful rooms, gorgeous views and fine dining. But the breathtaking setting of the Scottish Highlands, a fleet of Land Rovers at our disposal and all its sporting spaces makes Gleneagles a splurge I keep returning to.

Indeed, the approach to Gleneagles — with its 205 bedrooms and 28 suites, its acres and acres of hills, its carefully tended forests and gardens — feels like stepping onto the set of some great historical drama, like the swoon-worthy backdrops in “Outlander.”

When the hotel opened in 1924, the pure scale and opulence of it led London newspapers to hail Gleneagles as “the eighth wonder of the world.” Its Jazz Age concerts were so popular that they were broadcast over the new BBC “wireless” radio network. It wasn’t long before the hotel became a favorite retreat for royals and celebrities like Princess Margaret, Vivien Leigh and Sir Laurence Olivier.

To capture that 1920s magic and to celebrate our wedding anniversary, my husband and I took the overnight train earlier this summer from London to the hotel’s station.

I was already tired and cranky when we left at 11 p.m., and would have much preferred not to sleep on a train car, even a really, really nice one. In fact, the hotel was created by the Caledonian Railway as a way to capitalize on the growing popularity of train travel. “If you have the traveler in your pocket on the train, you might as well keep him,” the railway’s longtime general manager, Donald Matheson, had remarked.

But pulling up to Gleneagles — even at 6 a.m. — has always given me the feeling I was invited via hand-lettered invitation on heavy stock, instead of booking it online.

“You don’t arrive at Gleneagles so much as approach it — there’s a drive, and then a building that looks like it has been sitting there quite contentedly for a hundred years,” the actor Richard E. Grant, who co-hosts a podcast devoted to historic hotels, told me in an interview.

Invented in Scotland in the 15th century in its modern form, golf is still the hotel’s biggest draw. Jack Nicklaus designed the signature Centenary course, which hosted the Ryder Cup in 2014. During the hotel’s peak seasons, 11,500 rounds of golf are played a month.

And there are plenty of “pursuits” available: an equestrian school, as well as shooting, fishing, falconry, canoeing, kayaking, bouldering and rock climbing, among others. For the designer Rachelle Hruska, whose Lingua Franca clothing is sold on-site, the array of activities is the greatest draw. “Everything feels special without being overly fussy. It’s authentic and soulful — easier said than done,” she said.

Our celebratory visit began with a catered picnic. First we were driven to a reservoir in the hills in a Land Rover. Then a spread was set up like something out of a Nancy Meyers movie: fresh flowers, lobster, roast sirloin, an array of salads, fruit and a high tea selection of scones, jams and cream.

Despite the cost of £290 a person (about $360 each), the lunch didn’t seem to include any drinks other than water. We wanted wine, but we would’ve been happy with Arnold Palmers. The hotel later said we needed to have ordered additional beverages when we booked the picnic, but that hadn’t been clear to us. Next time, we’d opt for the basic picnic lunch to go (starting at £45 a person) and find a scenic spot on our own. But it was nice to try the fancy version.

On our previous trip to the hotel, I saved for six months to justify the splurge. Rooms average around £550 a night during low season and between £800 and £900 during the summer months and holidays. The New York Times, which does not accept free travel, paid about £4,000 for our three-night stay, which included meals and activities.

There was something distinctly upper class about how the hotel anticipated our every need and want. Fires blazed by the breakfast table when it was chilly, umbrellas appeared out of nowhere when there was a hint of rain.

And there was rain. To Mr. Grant, that only enhanced the atmospherics. “A misty day at Gleneagles isn’t a day ruined, it’s a day improved,” he said in an interview. “The hills go soft, sound comes closer, and the entire place turns the color of a photograph left too long in a drawer.”

Close to the reservoir sits a new sauna, where the view made me feel like I had been parachuted to the middle of nowhere. It’s housed in a beautiful Scandinavian-style cottage with the softest robes, a tea setup and lounge chairs. We had a lovely time in and out of the sauna, and relaxed on the deck without a person in sight. My husband even opted for a cold plunge in the reservoir, while I refrained.

When it came time to leave the sauna, I couldn’t stop staring out onto the reservoir and the miles and miles of hills beyond the property. I said something to Andrew Herd, the fishing instructor, about how the peace I feel in Scotland is really unlike anywhere else I’ve been. He smiled and said, “Well, Scotland is a country of 20 million acres and 5 million people. There’s just room to roam.”

His words stayed with me. The Gleneagles estate is spread over 850 acres, with 10 bars and restaurants, four pools and five outdoor tennis courts. A new indoor racquet club includes eight indoor tennis courts and three padel courts. We wandered in and out of the hotel, taking long walks through the fog after dinner and grabbing late-night drinks at the Art Deco-style American Bar, where Emilio, one of the bartenders made craft cocktails and told great stories.

During the day, we read books, took padel lessons and swam in the pool. We had a high-end whisky tasting with Krisztian Eke, the purveyor of the Still Room, a store featuring over 200 brands of single-malt whiskies. The most expensive? £45,000 a bottle.

My husband loved getting to sip some of the higher-end whiskies and learn about their stories. At the shops, I brought the hotel’s signature blueberry whisky jam as an anniversary gift. It only cost £8, but my husband adored it so much, you’d think I’d given him a vat of caviar.

I also swooned over the Lingua Franca sweaters, embroidered with Scottish-inspired phrases like “Don’t Give a Dram” and “Haste Ye Back.” But my favorite sweater said “Late Checkout Please.” I had just uttered those words that morning — it’s what I beg for at every hotel that steals my heart.

One morning I got up early to squeeze the most out of the day and tiptoed out of the room. As I walked down the long hallway, I couldn’t help but feel that I’d slipped into a scene from “Downton Abbey,” the 1920s edition.

The walls were a perfect shade of banker’s green, the ceilings were high with crown molding that looked like it went back generations. There were little velvet side chairs and benches every couple of hundred feet. As I approached the grand staircase to the lobby, I saw a pair of Chanel ballet flats strewed down the hall, as if someone had used them to play an impromptu game of horseshoes. The remnants, it seemed, of guests who’d had a much later night than we’d had.

I felt as I had when we first visited, that it wasn’t just hype: Gleneagles was built both for luxury and whimsy.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: Pilgrims to Flood-Stricken Nepal Sought the Divine at Sacred Mountain
item.description:
Many pilgrims to Mount Kailash, a sacred, snowcapped peak in the Himalayan region, only complete the trek once in their lifetime.

Making the trip to the remote mountainous region on the border of Nepal and Tibet can take months of planning, a small fortune and untold physical fortitude. The goal for those who make the journey is to take a step toward spiritual awakening on God’s doorstep.

When Amita Amin, 67, left her home in New York for Kailash this month, shepherding a small group of other local Hindu pilgrims, she was marking her seventh journey to the mountain — and her second trip this year.

“She believed in God so much,” said Aditi Patel, Ms. Amin’s daughter-in-law. “She just wanted to be close to his abode, as much as possible.”

Ms. Amin’s group was at the border on Wednesday morning, according to Dipak Lamicchane, who runs Trekking Planner Nepal, the tour company Ms. Amin uses on her trips. A flash flood triggered by glacial runoff ripped through the region about an hour after their last communication, he said from his home in Kathmandu, Nepal.

The group of pilgrims and their three Nepalese guides, including Mr. Lamicchane’s son-in-law, have not been heard from since.

Tens of thousands of tourists and pilgrims have already traveled to the area around Kailash this season, which runs from about May to September, Mr. Lamicchane said, because of colder weather during the rest of the year. Adventurers of all stripes visit the site, which regularly tops lists of the world’s best treks for its pristine natural beauty and rugged terrain.

The area is also sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs and those who follow the Bon tradition of Tibetan Buddhism. Visiting Kailash is not about conquering the mountain. It is about surrender, a belief that the journey itself draws pilgrims closer to the divine.

Hindus believe Mount Kailash is the home of Shiva, the god of destruction, transformation and meditation, and his wife, Parvati. The mountain is also an impressive topographical feature, a natural pyramid that slices 21,778 feet into blue Tibetan skies.

“It is generating an inner heat, Hindus would say,” said Dr. Steven Vose, a professor at the University of Colorado Denver who studies South Asian religious traditions. “That heat is transformative. It helps you step closer to enlightenment and liberation.”

A typical pilgrimage involves walking around the entirety of the mountain, about 33 miles, over several days. Snow melt from the mountain, which is believed to be so holy that attempts to summit its peak are banned, feeds Lake Manasarovar, also a holy site believed to be where Shiva bathes.

“If you’re auspicious enough,” said Dhruv Amin, Ms. Amin’s son, “you may even see him come down the mountain to bless you at night.”

Mr. Amin, 43, made the trip with his mother in 2010. He had already visited four sacred Hindu temples in India, and going to Kailash was a final pilgrimage before entering his medical residency. Trekking the mountain with his mother, he said, felt “as if God was watching us.”

“When I think of God,” Mr. Amin told The Times, “I think of the mountain.”

For Tibetan Buddhists, Mount Kailash is believed to be the dwelling place of a tantric deity, a place where pilgrims go to purify themselves, obtain blessings and advance their spiritual journey toward awakening.

Followers of Jainism, an Indian religion that aspires to spiritual purity and nonviolence, believe that their first spiritual teacher attained liberation by ascending the mountain. It is considered “the high-water mark of devotion, combined with yoga and asceticism,” Dr. Vose said.

In Sikhism, the mountain is said to be where the faith’s first guru undertook a famous dialogue with yogis of the Himalayas.

Kailash is “such a significant geographic and multi-faith landscape with spiritual potency,” said Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, a Sikh scholar and the chair of religious studies at Colby College in Maine. Ms. Singh’s mother’s name is Kailash.

Across all faiths, the journey to and around Mount Kailash was once only thought possible through mythical attainment. Even in the modern era, the trip remains arduous. Some pilgrims, particularly Tibetan Buddhists, enhance the already difficult journey by prostrating themselves the entire length of the trek.

“There is sacrifice involved,” said Dr. Jeffery D. Long, a professor of religion, philosophy and Asian studies at Elizabethtown College in Pennsylvania. “It adds to a sense of sanctity, humility, wearing down your ego.”

Ms. Amin did not anticipate making her latest pilgrimage to Kailash. But Tejal Patel, Ms. Patel's mother, had never made the journey and wanted to do so alongside family. About six months ago, the two women began planning. Ms. Patel, 64, started going to the gym.

A small group of other local Hindus decided to join them, preparing for the trip through video calls. Neelam and Ramesh Sharma, a couple from Queens, undertook the pilgrimage as part of their retirement. The pair, both in their 60s, have also not been heard from since the flood, their family said.

The risk involved in such a voyage was not lost on pilgrims like Ms. Amin. Before each trip, her son said, she would remark that it might be her last.

At least 675 deaths have been confirmed as a result of the catastrophic floods, and another 2,400 people were missing as of Saturday. More than 7,000 survivors have been rescued.

Mr. Amin wants to believe that his mother is stranded on the Chinese side of the border, where the bridge connecting China and Nepal has been destroyed and communication lines have been cut off. He hopes the group will be found, alive. That way, Ms. Amin can tell the tale of their miraculous survival, there at the door to God’s house.
